title: AMP: Adversarial Motion Priors for Stylized Physics-Based Character Control
summary: Adversarial motion rewards learn stylized task control and temporal skill selection from unstructured motion clips.
limitations: Mode collapse can discard useful styles. Priors are retrained per policy and acquire task dependencies through policy-generated data, limiting modular transfer. The study primarily tests temporal composition; spatial composition is future work. These simulator results do not establish held-out free-text combinations, detailed manipulation, or hardware transfer.
method: A discriminator learns motion-style rewards from state transitions in unstructured reference clips; PPO optimizes style plus engineered task rewards. Least-squares adversarial training, gradient penalty, and replay stabilize learning. Policies output PD joint targets without synchronizing to a selected reference clip; temporal skill selection emerges from the reward combination.
conditions: Character proprioception and task goals; style is specified by training motion examples. Unlike reference trackers, execution need not receive a time-indexed future reference. This is task-reward-conditioned control, without free-form language or an object-mesh-conditioned sequence generator.
data_split: Task-specific motion collections and per-task learning; no recording-disjoint composition train/test split. Single-clip imitation averages three training seeds and 32 episodes per model, each at most 20 seconds. The locomotion style collection has 56 clips from eight actors, not 56 independent skills.
metrics: Normalized task return measures objective fulfillment; DTW-aligned root-relative pose error measures single-clip resemblance. Learning curves assess efficiency and ablations. Task returns average three seeds/32 episodes; qualitative sequences demonstrate gait changes and skill transitions without a separate unseen-combination success metric.
evaluation: Demonstrates humanoid, dog, and T-Rex control. Crucially, the strike corpus contains only walking-only or punching-only clips: walk-then-punch emerges without a combined demonstration. Compares tracking-based imitation and ablates velocity features and gradient penalties; terrain and recovery examples extend task coverage.
evidence_locator: §§5–7 (discriminator/style rewards, PPO and tasks); §§8.1–8.2 and Tables 1–2 (three-seed task returns/corpora and walking-only/punching-only strike); §8.4 and Table 3 (DTW, 32 episodes, 20-second limit); §8.5/Figure 8 (ablations); §9 (mode collapse, transfer, spatial composition).
code_note: Current author project page links MimicKit as implementation; its README lists AMP. This current maintained implementation is not asserted byte-identical to the 2021 experiments.
publication_note: Published ACM TOG 40(4), 2021; inspected arXiv revision v2 is dated 12 May 2022. Publication year is 2021, not revision year 2022.

title: InterMimic: Towards Universal Whole-Body Control for Physics-Based Human-Object Interactions
publication_note: Author project page identifies CVPR 2025; this method audit specifically reads arXiv v2 dated 1 February 2026, including its supplementary material. Distinct from InterMimicGen.
method: Subject-specific RL teachers correct and retarget imperfect HOI to one canonical body using contact-aware rewards, physical-state initialization, and interaction early termination. Teacher rollouts supply refined state references and teacher actions supervise a student. A staged DAgger-to-PPO curriculum combines reference/action distillation with RL; a Transformer integrates reference keyframes.
conditions: Human/object states, joint-to-object geometry, simulated contact markers, and future reference human/object poses at specified offsets. Teachers use offsets {1,16}, students {1,2,4,16}. References come from MoCap, teacher rollouts, or a separate kinematic generator; text alone does not condition this tracker.
data_split: OMOMO has 17 subjects and 15 objects; teachers are subject-specific and subject 14 is held out from student training, with remaining subjects used to train the student. Irrecoverable references are filtered. No universal percentage or new semantic-combination holdout is declared; extra datasets primarily test teachers/qualitative transfer.
metrics: Success is the fraction of references imitated at least once; Duration measures time before termination. Human joint/object-point errors in centimeters use the best trial and tracked duration, excluding inaccurate hand joints on BEHAVE/OMOMO. These are reference-tracking metrics, not generated-motion text retrieval or task-success rates.
evaluation: Tables 1–2 compare PhysHOI/SkillMimic and distillation/PPO variants; test cases include subject 14, tenfold object masses, 24 ten-second HOI-Diff references and 60 InterDiff predictions (10 past/25 future frames). Unseen-object and multi-object transfer is also illustrated. Robot embodiment adaptation is simulated; hardware transfer is not established.
limitations: Reference lookahead remains required; generator composition is not autonomous semantic task discovery. Severe MoCap errors fail; unnatural penetration-based support and limited fine-finger dexterity remain. Robot experiments disable self-collision and model hand actuators differently from hardware. Best-trial tracking and held-out-student-subject results need separate interpretation.
evidence_locator: §3.1/Equation 1 (observations and GT reference goals); §§3.2–3.4/Algorithm 1 (teachers, reference/action distillation and schedule); §4 datasets/metrics and Tables 1–2 (subject 14, best-trial errors, external generators); §4.2/Figure 7 (object transfer) and supplementary F (multi-object extension); supplementary F (robot assumptions) and H (limitations).
summary: Subject-specific HOI teachers refine MoCap references, distill a shared reference-conditioned student, and improve it through RL fine-tuning.
